![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/d330e7c959ede9f969573752b9f67e3ce73c732a680b58cd2f9f466f1cf5db4c.png)

A conical container is $21\,\text{ft}$ tall with a diameter of $14\,\text{ft}.$ The container is being emptied so that the liquid level lowers at a rate of $2\,\text{ft/min}.$ At what rate is the liquid volume decreasing when the liquid level is $16\,\text{ft}?$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the container. Let's call $H=21\,\text{ft}$ the height of the conical container, and $R=\frac{14}{2}=7\,\text{ft}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the liquid level. We call $h$ the height of the liquid and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the liquid. Both of these quantities, and the liquid volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-2\,\text{ft}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to know $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=16\,\text{ft}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the container and the liquid must be similar. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{7}{21} \\ r & =\frac{1}{3}h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{1}{3}h)}^{2}h \\ v & =\frac{1}{27}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{27}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{9}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate at which the volume of water in the cup is changing when $h=16\,\text{ft}.$ 
So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{9}\pi (16)^{2}(-2) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & ≈-56.9\pi \,{\text{ft}}^{3}/\text{min}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

Therefore, the liquid volume decreases at a rate of approximately $56.9\pi \,\,{\text{ft}}^{3}\text{/min}.$
